lessons.title: Local Grains: Millett, Sorghum, and Maize for Beer and Gin
lessons.body:
In African brewing, local grains are your foundation. Millet, sorghum, and maize are readily available and cheap. For beer, you need to convert starch to sugar. Start by malting: soak grain in water for 12-24 hours, drain, and spread in a thin layer to germinate for 3-5 days. Keep it moist and turn daily. When sprouts are 1-2 cm, stop germination by drying in the sun or a low oven (50Â°C). This is your malt. For a 20-liter batch, use 4-5 kg of malt. Millett malt gives a dry, slightly tart beer; sorghum malt is smoother and often used in traditional opaque beers like umqombothi; maize malt adds sweetness but needs to be mixed with other grains for good conversion. 

Milling: Crush malt coarselyâyou want cracked grains, not flour. A corona mill or even a clean bottle as a roller works. 

Mashing: Heat 15 liters of water to 65-68Â°C. Add crushed malt, stir, and hold for 60-90 minutes. The enzymes convert starch to sugar. Test with iodine: a drop of wort on a white plate, add iodineâif it turns blue-black, starch remains; if yellow-brown, conversion is done. 

For gin, you don't need malt. You ferment a sugar wash (see Lesson 3) and distill. However, some gins use a small amount of malted grain for flavor. You can also make a 'grain bill' for gin by steeping unmalted grains in the wash for flavor. 

Tools: large pot (20L), thermometer, fermenter, siphon, airlock. 

Practical tip: If your beer tastes sour, it may be infected. Sanitize everything with a bleach solution (1 tablespoon per 4 liters) or boiling water. 

African context: In Nigeria, millet is used for 'burukutu'; in South Africa, sorghum for 'umqombothi'; in Kenya, maize for 'busaa'. These traditional beers are low-alcohol (2-4%) and often consumed fresh. For higher alcohol, add sugar or honey to the mash.

lessons.title: Fruits for Wine and Cider: Mango, Pineapple, Baobab, and Marula
lessons.body:
Fruit wines and ciders are perfect for African brewers because fruits are abundant and seasonal. The key is to extract juice, adjust sugar and acid, and ferment. 

Mango wine: Use ripe mangoes (5 kg for 20 liters). Peel, remove pits, and crush. Add 10 liters of water and 2 kg of sugar. Add 1 teaspoon of pectinase (optional, to break down pectin) and 1 crushed campden tablet (or 1/4 teaspoon potassium metabisulfite) to kill wild yeast. Wait 24 hours. Add wine yeast (e.g., Lalvin EC-1118). Ferment 7-10 days, then rack. 

Pineapple wine: Use 4 large pineapples. Peel and chop, simmer in 10 liters of water for 20 minutes to extract flavor. Strain, add 2 kg sugar, cool, and pitch yeast. Pineapple has natural acidity, so no need to add acid. 

Baobab wine: Baobab fruit pulp is dry and powdery. Mix 500g pulp with 10 liters water and 2 kg sugar. It's high in vitamin C and pectin. Add pectinase. Ferment with yeast. 

Marula wine: Marula fruits are high in sugar. Crush 10 kg ripe marula, add 5 liters water, and let wild ferment for 3 days (or add yeast). Strain and ferment. 

Cider: Use apples. Crush 10 kg apples, press juice. Add 1 kg sugar for stronger cider. Ferment with cider yeast (e.g., Nottingham Ale Yeast). 

Tools: fermenter, airlock, siphon, hydrometer (to measure sugar). 

Numbers: For 20 liters, aim for original gravity (OG) 1.080-1.100 for wine (12-14% ABV), 1.040-1.050 for cider (5-6% ABV). Use a hydrometer. 

African context: In West Africa, palm wine is a traditional fermented sap; in Southern Africa, marula is used for 'mampoer' (a brandy). Always sanitize. If you don't have commercial yeast, use wild yeast: leave juice uncovered for 2 days, then cover with cloth. But commercial yeast gives consistent results.

lessons.title: Sugar Sources: Cane Sugar, Honey, and Palm Wine Sap
lessons.body:
Sugar is the fuel for fermentation. In Africa, you have three main sources: cane sugar, honey, and palm wine sap. 

Cane sugar: The cheapest and most reliable. For 20 liters of wash, use 5-6 kg of white or brown sugar. Dissolve in hot water, then top up to 20 liters. This gives about 10-12% potential alcohol. For beer, you add sugar to boost alcohol; for wine, it's the main fermentable. 

Honey: Makes mead. Use 3-4 kg honey for 20 liters for a dry mead (12-14% ABV). Honey is expensive, so mix with cane sugar (1 kg honey + 2 kg sugar) to save money. Honey has natural wild yeast and antibacterial properties, so you must pasteurize (heat to 65Â°C for 30 minutes) or use campden tablets. 

Palm wine sap: Fresh sap from oil palm or raffia palm is already fermenting. You can collect it from a tapped tree. It contains 10-15% sugar and wild yeast. To make wine, drink fresh or let it ferment for 2-3 days for a bubbly, low-alcohol drink (4-6%). To distill for gin, ferment for 5-7 days to maximize alcohol, then distill. 

Practical: For a 20-liter batch, measure sugar with a hydrometer. Dissolve sugar in 5 liters hot water, add to fermenter, top up with cold water to 20 liters. Check OG. If OG is 1.080, you'll get ~10% ABV. 

Tools: large pot, stirring spoon, hydrometer, fermentation vessel. 

African context: In Nigeria, 'ogogoro' is distilled from palm wine; in Ghana, 'akpeteshie' from palm wine or sugar cane. In Ethiopia, 'tej' is honey wine. Always use clean water. If using honey, it may crystallizeâwarm gently. 

Warning: Don't use artificial sweetenersâyeast can't ferment them. Also, avoid sugar with preservatives (e.g., sulfur dioxide).

lessons.title: Yeast and Fermentation: Using Wild Yeast vs. Commercial Strains
lessons.body:
Yeast turns sugar into alcohol and CO2. You have two options: wild yeast or commercial strains. 

Wild yeast: Naturally present on fruit skins, grains, and in the air. To use, don't add any yeastâjust let the must sit uncovered for 2-3 days, then cover with a cloth. This works for traditional beers and wines. But it's unpredictable: may produce off-flavors, slow fermentation, or stuck batches. Wild yeast is best for low-alcohol, quick drinks like palm wine or traditional beer. 

Commercial yeast: Dried yeast strains like Saccharomyces cerevisiae (ale yeast, wine yeast, champagne yeast). For beer: use ale yeast (e.g., Safale US-05) at 18-22Â°C. For wine: use wine yeast (e.g., Lalvin EC-1118) at 20-25Â°C. For cider: use cider yeast. For gin wash: use distiller's yeast (e.g., Turbo Yeast) for high alcohol tolerance. 

Pitching: Sprinkle yeast on top of the must at 20-25Â°C. Do not stir. Wait 15 minutes, then stir gently. For 20 liters, use 5-10 grams of dry yeast. 

Fermentation: Primary fermentation takes 3-7 days for beer, 7-14 days for wine. Keep temperature stable. Use an airlock to let CO2 out and keep oxygen out. You'll see bubbles. When bubbling slows (1 bubble per minute), fermentation is nearly done. 

Testing: Use a hydrometer. Final gravity (FG) for beer: 1.010-1.015; wine: 0.990-1.000. If FG is stable for 2 days, fermentation is complete. 

Tools: airlock, bung, hydrometer, sanitizer. 

African context: In many African villages, wild yeast is used for 'pito' (Nigeria) or 'dolo' (Burkina Faso). Commercial yeast is available in cities at brewing supply shops or online. If you can't get commercial yeast, use baker's yeastâbut it gives a bread-like flavor. For best results, use a strain suited to your beverage. 

Tip: Rehydrate dry yeast in warm water (30Â°C) with a pinch of sugar for 10 minutes before pitching. This proves it's alive.

lessons.title: Water Treatment: Testing and Adjusting pH for Your Local Supply
lessons.body:
Water makes up 90% of your brew. Its pH and mineral content affect fermentation and flavor. 

Testing: Use a pH meter or pH strips. For beer mashing, target pH 5.2-5.6. For wine and cider, target pH 3.2-3.8. For gin wash, pH 5.0-5.5. If your water is too alkaline (pH >7), add acid. If too acidic (pH <5), add calcium carbonate (chalk). 

Adjusting: For 20 liters, add 1-2 teaspoons of gypsum (calcium sulfate) to lower pH and add calcium for yeast health. Add 1 teaspoon of lactic acid or citric acid to lower pH by 0.5. For raising pH, add 1 teaspoon of calcium carbonate. 

Chlorine: Tap water often has chlorine, which can create off-flavors. Remove by boiling for 15 minutes, or let sit uncovered for 24 hours, or add 1 campden tablet per 20 liters. 

Minerals: Yeast needs calcium, magnesium, zinc. If using distilled water, add yeast nutrient (1 teaspoon per 20 liters). 

Practical: Collect water from a well or borehole. Test pH. If pH is 7.5, add 1 teaspoon gypsum and 1/2 teaspoon citric acid. Stir, retest. Aim for 5.5 for beer. 

Tools: pH meter, gypsum, citric acid, campden tablets. 

African context: In many areas, water is hard (high minerals). That's okay for dark beers but can make wine taste harsh. If water is too hard, mix with rainwater (soft). Always boil water if you're unsure of its safety. 

Tip: For a 20-liter batch, start with 25 liters of waterâyou'll lose some to evaporation and absorption. 

Remember: If your brew tastes metallic or salty, your water is the problem. Adjust before you brew, not after.

lessons.title: Botanicals for Gin: African Wormwood, Rooibos, and Grains of Paradise
lessons.body:
Gin is a neutral spirit flavored with botanicals. In Africa, you have unique ingredients: African wormwood, rooibos, and grains of paradise. 

African wormwood (Artemisia afra): A bitter herb used in traditional medicine. Use 5-10 grams dried leaves per liter of distillate. It adds a bitter, herbal note. Soak in the spirit for 24 hours, then distill. 

Rooibos (Aspalathus linearis): A red bush tea from South Africa. Use 10-15 grams per liter. It gives a sweet, woody, and slightly floral flavor. Steep in the spirit before distillation or add to the still. 

Grains of Paradise (Aframomum melegueta): Also called alligator pepper. Use 5-8 grams per liter. It's peppery and citrusy. Crush lightly before use. 

Basic gin recipe: For 1 liter of 40% neutral spirit (from sugar wash or palm wine), add 10g juniper berries (essential), 5g coriander seeds, 2g African wormwood, 5g rooibos, 3g grains of paradise, and 1g orange peel. Soak for 24 hours. Distill in a pot still. Discard first 50 ml (foreshots) and last 100 ml (tails). Keep the middle run (hearts). Dilute to 40% with water. 

Tools: pot still, thermometer, hydrometer, glass jars. 

African context: In South Africa, 'gin' is often made with rooibos and citrus. In West Africa, grains of paradise are used in local gins. You can also add other local botanicals like hibiscus, ginger, or lemongrass. 

Practical: If you don't have a still, you can make a 'bathtub gin' by soaking botanicals in vodka for 1 week, then straining. But distillation gives a cleaner flavor. 

Tip: Start with small batches (1 liter) to adjust botanical ratios. Keep records. 

Safety: Distilling alcohol can be dangerousânever use a sealed pot. Always vent. Discard foreshots (methanol).

quiz.q: What is the first step to prepare local grains for brewing?
quiz.explanation: Malting involves soaking and germinating grains to develop enzymes needed for starch conversion.

quiz.q: Which grain is commonly used for traditional opaque beer like umqombothi?
quiz.explanation: Sorghum is the primary grain for umqombothi in South Africa.

quiz.q: How can you test if starch conversion is complete during mashing?
quiz.explanation: Iodine turns blue-black if starch is present; yellow-brown means conversion is done.

quiz.q: What is the recommended temperature range for mashing grains?
quiz.explanation: 65-68Â°C is optimal for enzyme activity that converts starch to sugar.

quiz.q: Which fruit is high in natural acidity and requires no added acid for wine?
quiz.explanation: Pineapple has sufficient natural acidity for winemaking.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of adding pectinase to fruit wine?
quiz.explanation: Pectinase breaks down pectin, improving clarity and juice extraction.

quiz.q: How much sugar is typically needed for 20 liters of wine to reach 12-14% ABV?
quiz.explanation: About 4-5 kg of sugar yields 12-14% alcohol in 20 liters.

quiz.q: Which yeast is recommended for high-alcohol washes for gin?
quiz.explanation: Turbo yeast tolerates high alcohol and ferments quickly.

quiz.q: What is a key difference between wild yeast and commercial yeast?
options: B) Commercial yeast is more predictable
C) Wild yeast produces higher alcohol
quiz.explanation: Commercial yeast strains are selected for consistent fermentation and flavor.

quiz.q: What is the typical original gravity range for wine?
quiz.explanation: OG 1.080-1.100 is standard for wine, yielding 12-14% ABV.

quiz.q: Which sugar source is already fermenting when collected?
quiz.explanation: Palm wine sap contains wild yeast and begins fermenting immediately.

quiz.q: How much honey is needed for 20 liters of dry mead?
quiz.explanation: 3-4 kg honey gives a dry mead of about 12-14% ABV.

quiz.q: What is 'ogogoro' in Nigeria?
options: B) A distilled spirit from palm wine
quiz.explanation: Ogogoro is a traditional distilled spirit made from palm wine.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid artificial sweeteners in fermentation?
options: A) They are toxic to yeast
quiz.explanation: Artificial sweeteners are non-fermentable, so they don't contribute alcohol.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an airlock in fermentation?
options: B) Release CO2 and prevent oxygen entry
quiz.explanation: An airlock allows CO2 to escape while keeping oxygen out.

quiz.q: What is the typical final gravity for beer?
quiz.explanation: Beer typically finishes at FG 1.010-1.015.

quiz.q: Which water treatment removes chlorine?
quiz.explanation: Boiling drives off chlorine gas.

quiz.q: What is the target pH for beer mashing?
quiz.explanation: Mash pH 5.2-5.6 is optimal for enzyme activity.

quiz.q: Which mineral is commonly added to lower pH and provide yeast nutrients?
quiz.explanation: Gypsum (calcium sulfate) lowers pH and adds calcium.

quiz.q: What should you do if your water is too hard for brewing?
quiz.explanation: Rainwater is soft and can dilute hard water minerals.

quiz.q: Which botanical is essential for gin?
quiz.explanation: Juniper berries are the defining flavor of gin.

quiz.q: What is the role of African wormwood in gin?
quiz.explanation: African wormwood contributes a bitter, herbal note.

quiz.q: How much rooibos is recommended per liter of distillate?
quiz.explanation: 10-15 g rooibos per liter gives a balanced flavor.

quiz.q: What are grains of paradise also known as?
quiz.explanation: Grains of paradise are also called alligator pepper.

quiz.q: What should you discard during distillation?
quiz.explanation: Foreshots contain methanol and tails have off-flavors; both are discarded.

quiz.q: What is a safe alternative to distillation for making gin at home?
quiz.explanation: Soaking botanicals in vodka infuses flavor without distillation.

quiz.q: Which of these is a traditional African fermented beverage?
quiz.explanation: Tej is an Ethiopian honey wine.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for rehydrating dry yeast?
quiz.explanation: 30Â°C is optimal for rehydrating yeast without killing it.

quiz.q: Which tool measures sugar content in wort or must?
quiz.explanation: A hydrometer measures specific gravity, indicating sugar content.

quiz.q: What is the recommended sanitizer for brewing equipment?
quiz.explanation: A dilute bleach solution (1 tbsp per 4 liters) sanitizes equipment.
